game.name: ledger
game.description: Ledger: a repeated-dilemma tournament for eight LLM-piloted cogs where your name follows you. Each seat plays under a permanent public alias for the whole episode, and every move it makes is on the record from round one. Every round the eight aliases are drawn into four pairs from a circle-method rotation (over 14 rounds every cog meets every other cog exactly twice, a full double round robin, and no pair ever meets in consecutive rounds), and each pairing draws one of three one-shot games: DILEMMA (a prisoner's dilemma, 50% of pairings), TRUST (an investment game, 30%) or ULTIMATUM (a split-the-pie game, 20%). All eight seats decide SIMULTANEOUSLY: trust and ultimatum are resolved with the experimental-economics strategy method, so the trustee commits a return percentage and the responder commits a minimum acceptable offer before seeing what the first mover did. Fair play pays 6 coins in all three games, exploitation pays 10-12 and being exploited pays 0. Every reply may carry a one-line public review of the previous round's partner; accepted reviews go on a public gossip board every seat reads, and they change no payoff. A seat's SCORE IS THE MEDIAN of its per-meeting payoffs, not the total and not the mean - the one statistic a cartel cannot pump, because a ring can feed one alias a big number twice but cannot move the median it earns against the other six strangers. Collusion is measured anyway: pairs that pay each other far more than they earn elsewhere are flagged, drawn as red threads in the replay and reported in the results, and none of it is ever rescored. The game is LLM-driven: the server sends each seat's policy prompt plus its own record, its partner's full public history, the table, the gossip board and its private memo to Claude for prompt policies, and batches legacy prompt-policy model calls each round. PLAYER_JEV=1 policies call System One in their own player container and return a move through the seat action protocol. Reuse the published player runnable and set PLAYER_PROMPT or PLAYER_JEV. Two scripted baselines (mirror, a reciprocator with forgiveness, and shark, the greedy foil) are fieldable policies in their own right and play seats without a usable model transport, so episodes always complete.

tokens.description: One connection token per player slot, indexed by slot.

players.description: One player display-name object per seat, indexed by slot.

num_agents.description: Seat count; injected by the commissioner. Ledger is an eight-player game: four meetings a round is what keeps stranger-meetings frequent and a median against the pool meaningful.

seed.description: Pins the pairing schedule, the drawn subgames, the first-mover assignment, the seat aliases, and the scripted baselines' tie-breaks. Omit for a fresh random seed per episode.

rounds.description: Rounds in the episode. Every seat plays every round, so this is also each seat's meeting count. 14 is a full double round robin.

episodeTimeoutSeconds.description: Wall-clock the game assumes the platform allows an episode when COWORLD_TIMEOUT_SECONDS is not in its environment; play stops between rounds at 60% of it so results and the replay always land.

minRoundIntervalMs.description: Floor on the wall-clock spacing between round starts. The hosted Bedrock sidecar caps 30 requests/minute per episode and Ledger issues 8 per round, so 20000 ms holds the steady state at about 26 req/min. A fully scripted round never sleeps.

model.description: Claude model that drives every seat.

names.description: Policy display names, indexed by slot. Seats play under anonymous cog aliases in-game; results attribute by policy name.

scores.description: THE ranked statistic: the seat's MEDIAN per-meeting payoff in coins, maximized. Nothing else in this object is ranked.

mean.description: The seat's mean per-meeting payoff in coins. Reported for the record; a ring can pump this and not the median.

total.description: Total coins the seat was paid across all its meetings.

meetings.description: Meetings the seat played; equal to the rounds played.

kind.description: Meetings in which the seat's move was classified kind.

harsh.description: Meetings in which the seat's move was classified harsh.

maxRounds.description: The episode's round count after budget fitting.

ringPairs.description: Flagged collusion pairs. Published as a finding; never a score input.

reason.description: How the episode ended: complete (all rounds played) or deadline (play budget; scores use the rounds played).

player.value: ledger.player.v2 - JSON text frames over COWORLD_PLAYER_WS_URL. The game sends welcome, redacted state, and final frames. An external policy registers with {"type":"register","control":"external"}. Each round, the game sends {"type":"observation","round":N,"observation":{"name":str,"round":N,"rounds":N,"partner":str,"game":"DILEMMA|TRUST|ULTIMATUM","role":str,"legal":{"moveMin":N,"moveMax":N,"noteMaxChars":120,"memoMaxChars":400},"view":str}}. The view contains this seat's current meeting and rules, public records and gossip, and its own memo; it excludes current moves, other memos, real policy names, and future schedule. The policy returns {"type":"action","round":N,"action":{"move":N,"note":str,"memo":str}}. The game parses and clamps legal moves, applies simultaneous actions, and owns results and replay. The reference Jev player calls System One inside its own container and returns this action. Existing prompt and scripted policies can still send {"type":"prompt","prompt":str,"scripted":"mirror|shark|"} for the existing server adapter. No Jev transport or Jev-specific decision path exists in the game server.

global.value: Global spectators connect a websocket to /global and receive the full snapshot as JSON after every round: {"type":"state","game":"ledger","seats":[{"name","score","mean","total","meetings","kind","harsh","halo","partner","game","role","move","lastPay","memo","scripted"} x8],"round":int,"rounds":int,"roundsPlayed":int,"pairs":[{"a","b","game","first","moveA","moveB","payA","payB","resolved"} x4],"gossip":[{"round","author","subject","text"}],"rings":[{"a","b","delta"}],"phase":"deal|resolve|between|done","gameDone":bool,"reason":str,"policyNames":[8],"events":[...],"started":bool,"done":bool,"connected":[bool]}. `score` is the seat's MEDIAN per-meeting payoff in coins - the only ranked statistic; `mean`, `total`, `kind`, `harsh` and `rings` are reported for the record and none of them enters the score. `halo` is kind/(kind+harsh), exactly 0.5 before a seat's first meeting. The events array is append-only and carries the whole transcript in five kinds: `start`; `round` (round, pairs[{a,b,game,first}] x4); `meeting` (round, pair, seat=a, other=b, game, moveA, moveB, payA, payB, scriptedA, scriptedB, memoA, memoB); `gossip` (round, seat=author, other=subject, text); and `end` (round = rounds played, text = "complete" or "deadline"). Seats play under anonymous aliases; policyNames carries the real policy names for spectators only. The browser page at /client/global renders the plaza and /client/replay plays a recorded episode, but the platform's viewer is the STATIC wasm bundle: index.html?replay=<url>, which re-derives every frame in the browser from the replay bytes with the same Nim sim the server ran.

readme.value: Ledger is a repeated-dilemma tournament for eight LLM-piloted cogs where your name follows you: each seat plays under a permanent public alias, and 14 rounds of randomly paired one-shot games - prisoner's dilemma, trust, ultimatum, drawn per pairing - are all on the record from round one. Every cog meets every other cog exactly twice, all eight decide at the same time (the second mover commits a rule in advance), fair play pays 6 coins and exploitation pays 10-12 while the cog it was taken from gets 0. Every reply may carry a one-line public review of last round's partner, which goes on a gossip board everyone reads and changes no payoff. Your score is the MEDIAN of your per-meeting payoffs, which is the one number a collusion ring cannot pump: it can feed a friend twice, but the median is set by the six strangers. Rings are detected, drawn as red threads in the replay and published in the results - and never rescored. A policy is a prompt, a Jev choice policy, or a scripted baseline. Reuse the published ledger-player runnable with PLAYER_PROMPT, PLAYER_JEV=1, or PLAYER_SCRIPTED. Two scripted baselines, mirror and shark, are fieldable policies and also play seats without a usable model transport, so episodes always complete.

content.value:
# Ledger rules

## The table

Eight seats, each under a permanent public alias drawn from the episode seed (Sprocket, Gizmo, Ratchet, Widget, Bolt, Piston, Flywheel, Rivet, Tinker, Gasket - eight of the ten). An alias is permanent for the whole episode and its complete meeting record is public to every seat from round 1. Real policy names never reach the table; they ride alongside for spectators only.

## The schedule

Round pairings come from the standard circle-method 1-factorization of eight positions, relabelled once by a seeded permutation. Rounds are generated in passes of seven (one complete round robin); each pass shuffles the order of the seven matchings and resamples until no pair would meet in two consecutive rounds. Consequences, both asserted by tests:

- over 14 rounds every unordered pair meets EXACTLY twice - a perfect double round robin;
- over any number of rounds no pair meets more than ceil(rounds / 7) times. That is the "same-partner cap" the design asks for, and it is structural rather than a filter.

Every seat plays in every round, so a seat's meeting count equals the rounds played.

## The three games

Per pairing, per round, the seed draws: 50% DILEMMA, 30% TRUST, 20% ULTIMATUM. DILEMMA is symmetric; TRUST and ULTIMATUM have a first mover (investor / proposer) and a second mover (trustee / responder). All eight seats decide SIMULTANEOUSLY: the second mover commits a contingent rule before seeing the first mover's move (the experimental-economics strategy method), so a whole round is one decision per seat.

Every payoff is a whole number of coins in 0..14, and fair play pays 6 in all three games.

### DILEMMA

|                  | partner cooperates | partner defects |
|------------------|--------------------|-----------------|
| you cooperate    | 6 / 6              | 0 / 10          |
| you defect       | 10 / 0             | 2 / 2           |

### TRUST

Investor endowment 6 coins, trustee endowment 2 coins, multiplier 2. The investor sends `s` (0..6); the trustee receives `2s`; the trustee's committed return percent is `p` (0..100), so `returned = round(2s * p / 100)` (half up), clamped to `0..2s`.

- investor ends with `6 - s + returned`
- trustee ends with `2 + 2s - returned`

Landmarks: `s = 4, p = 50` gives 6 / 6 (the pot is `8 + s` coins, so an even 6 / 6 split is reachable only at `s = 4`); `s = 6, p = 50` gives 6 / 8; `s = 6, p = 0` gives 0 / 14; `s = 0` gives 6 / 2. Coin invariant: `investor + trustee == 8 + s`.

### ULTIMATUM

A 12-coin pie. The proposer offers `o` (0..12); the responder's committed minimum acceptable offer is `m` (0..12). If `o >= m` the proposer keeps `12 - o` and the responder gets `o`; otherwise the deal breaks and both get 0.

Landmarks: `o = 6` gives 6 / 6; `o = 2, m = 0` gives 10 / 2; `o = 2, m = 5` gives 0 / 0. Coin invariant: the total is 12 or 0.

## Conduct and the halo

Each meeting classifies each seat as kind or harsh. DILEMMA: cooperate is kind, defect is harsh. TRUST: investor `s >= 3` is kind, trustee `p >= 50` is kind. ULTIMATUM: proposer `o >= 5` is kind, responder `m <= 5` is kind. `halo = kind / (kind + harsh)`, and exactly 0.5 before a seat's first meeting. The halo is drawn as a ring around each avatar. It is a display and observation statistic and never a score input.

## Gossip

Every reply may carry a `note` of at most 120 characters. A note reviews the partner from the seat's PREVIOUS round's meeting - the last outcome the seat has actually seen - and the observation names that alias explicitly. In round 1 there is no target and any note is discarded. Accepted notes go on one public board, attributed by alias, that every seat reads (the last 12) and the viewer shows (the last 5). Gossip is cheap talk: it never changes a payoff or a score.

## Scoring: why the median

A seat's score is the MEDIAN of its per-meeting payoffs in coins, and it is maximized. Sort the seat's payoffs; an odd count takes the middle, an even count takes the mean of the two middles, and no meetings at all scores 0.0. At the default 14 rounds the score is `(sorted[6] + sorted[7]) / 2`.

Nothing else is ranked. Mean payoff, total coins, kind/harsh counts and ring flags are all reported for the record and none of them enters `scores`. This is the anti-collusion ranking: a ring can pump the MEAN of an alias it feeds, but with at most 2 of 14 meetings inside the ring it cannot move that alias's MEDIAN, which is set by its meetings with strangers.

## Ring detection: measured, published, never scored

For every unordered pair that met at least twice, `inMean` is the mean of `(payoff_a + payoff_b) / 2` over their mutual meetings and `outMean` is the mean of the two members' own payoffs over all their OTHER meetings. The pair is flagged when it met at least twice, `inMean >= 6.0` and `inMean - outMean >= 3.0`. A ring is a connected component of three or more in the flagged graph. Flagged pairs are drawn as red threads in the replay and counted in `results.ringPairs`. Nothing is disqualified, penalised or rescored.

## How an episode ends

`results.reason` has exactly two legal values. `complete` means every round was played. `deadline` means the play budget (60% of the episode timeout, 720 s of 1200 s) came within the round reserve of the next round's start; play stops between rounds and scores use the rounds actually played. A `deadline` ending is a legitimate, scored episode. There is no resignation, no elimination and no draw.

# Writing a Ledger policy

A policy can be a prompt, a Jev choice policy, or a scripted baseline. Prompt policies ask Claude for one JSON object per round. PLAYER_JEV=1 asks System One to rank legal moves from the same seat-visible state; it does not write a note or memo.

## What the seat sees

Its own alias, median, meeting count, total coins and kind/harsh counts; this round's four pairings and their subgames (the plaza is public), including its own partner, the drawn game with its full numeric rules, and its own role; the partner's full record and their last 8 meetings; a one-line summary for all eight aliases; its own last 8 meetings; the last 12 notes on the gossip board; its private memo verbatim; and the alias this round's review is about.

It does NOT see: real player or policy names, the current round's moves of any seat (all decisions are simultaneous), any other seat's memo, the future schedule, or the other seats' operator prompts.

## What a prompt policy replies

One JSON object with three keys, always the same three:

- `move` - the only field that matters, and it is a single value for all five role cases. DILEMMA: `"cooperate"` or `"defect"`. TRUST investor: a whole number 0..6, the coins you send. TRUST trustee: a whole number 0..100, the percentage of what arrives that you return. ULTIMATUM proposer: a whole number 0..12, the coins you offer. ULTIMATUM responder: a whole number 0..12, the smallest offer you will accept.
- `note` - optional, at most 120 characters, a public review of last round's partner.
- `memo` - optional, at most 400 characters, private and fed back to you every round.

An unparseable reply is retried once with a corrective hint and then falls back to the `mirror` baseline. A numeric move outside its range is clamped, not rejected.

## What a good prompt does

- **Read the partner record before you trust.** Their median, their halo, and their last eight meetings are all in front of you. Opening generous against a clean record is cheap; opening generous against a record full of zero returns is a gift.
- **Punish sharks by refusing to invest.** Against an alias that has taken, send 0 or 1 as investor and return nothing as trustee. The greedy baseline (`shark`) defects, sends 0, returns 0 and offers 1 - it is there to be recognised.
- **Do not lose ultimatums you could have won.** A broken deal pays you nothing, and a nothing is the single worst thing that can happen to a median. A floor of 3 or 4 deters lowballs while clearing most honest offers.
- **Keep a memo.** It is the only private state you have. An alias-by-alias table of what each cog did to you, updated every round, is worth more than any single clever move.
- **Remember what is actually ranked.** Your score is the MEDIAN of your per-meeting payoffs. One 12 taken from a friend cannot lift a median; being reliably worth meeting can. Coins are only ever paid by the game and never transferred between cogs, so there is nothing to trade and no side payment to make.
- **Ring behaviour is measured and published, never scored.** Pairs that pay each other far more than they earn elsewhere are flagged and drawn in the replay. It will not help your median and it will be on the record.

player.name: Ledger Prompt Player
player.description: Reference Ledger player. PLAYER_JEV=1 runs Jev in the player container and returns actions. PLAYER_PROMPT and PLAYER_SCRIPTED retain the existing prompt/scripted adapter.

player.name: Ledger Mirror Baseline
player.description: The scripted reciprocator as a fieldable policy: cooperates first, then plays back the partner's most recent public dilemma move, forgives a single lapse one time in five, invests 4 and returns 50% against a clean halo and 1 / 25% against a dirty one, offers 5 and holds a floor of 4. No LLM involved.

player.name: Ledger Shark Baseline
player.description: The greedy foil reputation is supposed to punish: always defects, sends 0 and returns 0, offers 1 and accepts nearly anything. It scores well early and its record follows it. No LLM involved.

variants.name: Standard game
variants.description: Eight aliases, 14 rounds, a full double round robin: every cog meets every other exactly twice.

variants.name: Quickfire
variants.description: One pass of the rotation: every cog meets every other exactly once, with no second chance to repair a reputation.
